# Ambient and high-temperature rotating bending fatigue of as-built and hot isostatic pressed additively manufactured 316L stainless steel

## Abstract

This study investigates the effects of Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) on the rotating bending fatigue (RBF) performance of Powder Bed Fused-Laser Beam (PBF-LB) 316L stainless steel (SS316L) at both room (25 °C) and elevated temperatures (450 °C). HIP was applied at 1150 °C and 100 MPa for 4 h following stress relief to eliminate porosity and homogenize the microstructure. Advanced microstructural characterization revealed that HIP reduced porosity below detection limits and transformed the melt-pool structure into an equiaxed grain morphology with a significant increase in Σ3 twin boundary fraction (∼2.4 % to 33 %). These changes were accompanied by reduced dislocation density and internal strain. Fatigue testing showed that HIP specimens exhibited superior high-temperature fatigue endurance (170 MPa) compared to as-built samples (130 MPa), due to defect elimination and microstructural stabilization. However, at 25 °C, as-built specimens outperformed HIP ones (240 MPa vs. 220 MPa) owing to retained work-hardened microstructures. Fractographic analysis confirmed these trends: multiple crack initiation sites dominated as-built failures, while HIP fractures showed single-origin cracks with striation growth. Post-fatigue electron backscatter diffraction maps revealed temperature-dependent grain coarsening and dislocation accumulation, particularly in the as-built samples. Overall, HIP significantly enhanced the high-temperature fatigue resistance of PBF-LB_SS316L by improving microstructural integrity and delaying crack initiation, highlighting the importance of post-processing in AM components.

## 1. Introduction

Stainless steel 316L (SS316L) is one of the most widely used alloys in industry, particularly for applications requiring high mechanical strength and corrosion resistance [[1], [2], [3]]. The Powder Bed Fused-Laser Beam (PBF-LB) additive manufacturing (AM) process offers precise control over production parameters, enabling the optimization of microstructure and properties beyond those of conventionally manufactured SS316L. Several studies [[4], [5], [6]] have demonstrated the potential for performance enhancement through PBF-LB. For instance, Li et al. [7] achieved an ultimate tensile strength of 651 MPa and 62 % elongation using a 210 W laser, a scanning speed of 1000 mm/s, and a 30 μm layer thickness, followed by annealing heat treatment. Xu et al. [4] reported that PBF-LB_SS316L samples reached a density exceeding 99.2 %, resulting in a strength of approximately 670 MPa. Additionally, Yousef et al. [8] showed that altering the build orientation in PBF-LB affects corrosion resistance. Despite these advancements, one of the most critical requirements for SS316L, particularly in industrial applications involving rolled components, is fatigue resistance under various operating conditions and temperatures.

## 2. Experimental procedure

### 2.1. Materials and methods

In this study, SS316L powder with an average particle size of 37 ± 5 μm and a nominal chemical composition of Cr:16.5–18.5, Mo:2.0–2.5, Mn: ≤2.0, Ni: 10–13, Si: ≤1.0, C: 0–0.03 wt%, and Fe as the base was utilized. Fatigue test samples were designed with two distinct geometries to accommodate testing at both elevated (Fig. 1a) and ambient (Fig. 1b) temperatures.

The samples were fabricated using the PBF-LB process on a GE M2 machine, with process parameters including a laser power of 370 W, a scanning speed of 1350 mm/s, a hatch spacing of 90 μm, a layer thickness of 50 μm, and a laser spot size of 130 μm under constant purge of nitrogen gas (No contouring strategy was applied during fabrication, as the focus of this study was to investigate the bulk fatigue behavior and microstructural response of PBF-LB SS316L in as-built and HIP conditions, without the influence of additional surface-related processing variables) Fig. 1c shows the schematic of the PBF-LB method used to produce fatigue samples. Fig. 1, Fig. 1 illustrate the build plate, including ambient and elevated temperature samples, respectively. Following fabrication, all specimens underwent a stress relief heat treatment at 550 °C for 6 h (Fig. 2a) before being separated from the build plate. After stress-relieving both build plates, the specimens were extracted (Fig. 2b), and a subset from each series was selected for the HIP process.

The HIP process was conducted at 100 MPa and 1150 °C for 4 h, following the ASTM F3184:2024 standard (Fig. 2c). After HIP, the samples were rapidly cooled using argon gas to minimize thermal effects. Uniaxial tensile stress–strain curves before and after the HIP process for PBF-LB_SS316L were extracted.

Fatigue testing was performed using the RBF method at both ambient temperature and at 450 °C, utilizing a Zwick Amsler RBM120T system equipped with an in-situ furnace for high-temperature testing. It is noted that RBF introduces a stress gradient across the gauge section, with the maximum stress localized at the specimen surface. As such, the obtained fatigue limits are not directly equivalent to those from axial fatigue tests. The rotating-bending method was selected due to facility availability and because it accentuates surface-driven fatigue mechanisms, which are particularly relevant in PBF-LB 316L stainless steel. The applied stress during fatigue tests ranged from 86 % to 40 % of the yield strength, and corresponding RBF test results were generated for all samples following ISO 1143 guidelines [38]. The RBF was performed on an in-situ furnace, maintaining the specimen at 450 °C, following ASTM E606:2021 [39]. This was justified by relevant studies on the high-temperature performance of SS316L components such as pressure vessels, heat exchangers, superheater tubes, and gas turbine parts, including impellers and blades [33]. In all RBF tests, runout was defined a priori as survival without fracture to N ≥ 5.0 × 10^{6} cycles (fully reversed bending, R =  − 1).

To enable like-for-like comparisons across built conditions and temperatures, the nominal bending stresses for all RBF tests were defined to be consistent on a normalized basis. At 25 °C, target amplitudes were chosen to span comparable fractions of the measured room temperature yield strength for both as-built and HIP conditions, so that any differences in the S–N response reflect microstructural effects rather than normalization. For 450 °C, target amplitudes were normalized to an estimated elevated temperature yield strength (450 °C), obtained by calibrating a standard temperature softening relation for steels to the published 600 °C tensile curve of PBF-LB_SS316L from Dryepondt et al. [40] (see Fig. 6a). It should be noted that the reference σ_{y} used for normalization at 450 °C is not an experimentally measured value at this temperature, but rather an estimated strength obtained by extrapolating published 600 °C tensile data within a physically based softening framework. Because we did not perform high-temperature uniaxial tensile tests, this external curve (embedded in a physically based softening framework) served only to set a conservative, mechanistically justified scale for σ_{y}(T). In each test series, a small number of preliminary tests were conducted; thereafter, the stress amplitude was reduced stepwise based on observed results until the runout criterion was reached. This protocol was applied identically to as-built and HIP specimens at both temperatures.

The fracture surfaces of the tested samples were thoroughly analyzed using an SEM at various magnifications to investigate crack initiation and propagation leading to failure. Microstructural modifications at the fracture edges were assessed using the EBSD method. It is important to note that all calculations and measurements in this study were conducted with an uncertainty assessment at a 95 % confidence level, employing a coverage factor K = 2, with each measurement repeated a minimum of three times.

### 3.4. High and ambient temperature fatigue behavior

#### 3.4.1. S-N curve

Fig. 7 reveals significant differences in fatigue performance among the four conditions, in both the endurance limit (horizontal asymptote of the S-N curve) and the slope of the fatigue life curve in the finite-life regime. At ambient temperature, the as-built material showed superior HCF strength compared to its HIP samples, as shown by the blue symbols in Fig. 7. The as-built specimens represent the reference S-N curve from the authors' previous study [66]. In contrast, the HIP samples tested at 25 °C (red symbols) endured a slightly lower stress of around 220 MPa for the same fatigue life (at a runout cycle of 5×106). In other words, under room-temperature conditions, the as-built state maintains a higher fatigue limit than the HIP post-processed state, despite the latter’s elimination of internal porosity. This behavior appears to contradict the conventional understanding of HIP treatment, which typically enhances fatigue performance by reducing internal porosities that act as crack initiation sites. However, this discrepancy can be attributed to the fundamental difference between RBF and uniaxial fatigue tests. In RBF testing, the surface layer experiences the highest tensile stress and plays a dominant role in crack initiation, making it a surface-sensitive fatigue method. Since HIP primarily affects subsurface and internal defects but has limited influence on surface imperfections, the process may not significantly improve surface integrity. The individual data points used to construct Fig. 7, including the applied stress levels and corresponding number of cycles to failure for each condition, are listed in Table 1. Consequently, the as-built specimens, which were polished and retained their original surface characteristics, exhibited superior fatigue strength compared to the HIP samples.

By contrast, the HIP samples at 450 °C (green symbols) demonstrated a much higher endurance strength of about 170 MPa, and their S-N curve was considerably flatter in the HCF regime. Even at 450 °C, the HIP material retained a well-defined fatigue limit (runouts at 170 MPa) and sustained significantly longer lives at a given stress amplitude compared to the as-built material. In summary, whereas elevated temperature caused a dramatic 45 % drop in the endurance limit of the as-built alloy (240 to 130 MPa) alongside a steep S-N slope, the HIP alloy experienced only a relatively modest 15 % reduction in endurance limit (220 to 170 MPa) and preserved a gentle S-N slope with a discernible fatigue threshold.

This study's fatigue data were obtained in RBF per ISO 1143, which creates a fully reversed stress state that peaks at the surface and decreases toward the neutral axis [38]. Because only a small surface volume experiences the maximum alternating stress each cycle, RBF is not directly equivalent to uniform-stress axial fatigue as defined in ASTM E466 [68]. The green S-N curve retains a broad plateau out to 5×106 cycles and only gradually declines at higher stress amplitudes, indicating that fatigue failure in the HIP/450 °C condition is controlled more by the inherent strength of the thermally softened austenitic matrix and the effective microstructural barriers (twin-enhanced grain boundaries) rather than by catastrophic defect-driven crack initiation. In practical terms, the HIP process has preserved a large fraction of the material’s ambient fatigue capability even at 450 °C, whereas the as-built material’s capability has nearly collapsed in that regime. The evolution of fatigue mechanisms with temperature (from primarily defect-governed crack initiation at ambient, to creep-assisted and microstructure-governed failure at 450 °C) is tempered by the HIP-induced improvements in microstructural integrity. This understanding underscores that a combined strategy of pore elimination (via HIP) and microstructural optimization is crucial for ensuring reliable fatigue performance of PBF-LB SS316L, especially for service at elevated temperatures.

The combination of low dislocation density, a recrystallized equiaxed grain structure, and abundant twin boundaries effectively suppressed creep-assisted fatigue damage, even at 450 °C. Furthermore, comparing the HIP 450 °C data (green curve) to the baseline 25 °C data (blue and red curves) highlights the remarkable preservation of fatigue strength after HIP, even under severe thermal exposure. Unlike the as-built condition, where high temperatures drastically reduced fatigue life, the HIP material retained a significant proportion of its ambient fatigue life. A reference is provided in the fatigue behavior of PBF-LB_SS316L.

At the elevated temperature (450 °C), additional fatigue damage mechanisms (such as dislocation climb and grain-boundary sliding) become operative [18,80]. The as-built sample, with its high residual stresses, elongated grains, and heavily deformed microstructure, is particularly vulnerable to accelerated fatigue, leading to premature failure. In contrast, the HIP sample, characterized by a stress-relieved, recrystallized, and equiaxed grain structure, exhibited enhanced resistance to creep-fatigue damage. The high density of Σ3 twin boundaries further restricted grain boundary sliding, a critical mechanism in high-temperature fatigue, thereby providing additional resistance.


At elevated temperatures, the performance trend reversed in comparison with room temperature samples. The as-built microstructure underwent accelerated degradation due to thermally activated processes such as grain coarsening, pore coalescence, and enhanced dislocation mobility. These phenomena, combined with pre-existing residual stresses and microstructural inhomogeneity, contribute to faster crack initiation and propagation. In contrast, the HIP sample, with its homogenized and densified microstructure, exhibited superior thermal stability. Despite increased plastic deformation and dislocation accumulation, the absence of initial porosity and the inherently stress-relieved condition inhibited premature crack nucleation. Furthermore, the more uniform grain structure of HIP samples resisted localized strain accumulation, delaying fatigue damage under high-temperature cyclic loadings. Thus, the enhanced fatigue resistance of HIP samples at elevated temperatures stems from their superior thermal stability, reduced defect population, and more homogeneous microstructural response to mechanical and thermal stimuli.

## 5. Summary and conclusions

This study comprehensively assessed the impact of Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) on the rotating bending fatigue (RBF) behavior of PBF-LB_SS316L at both ambient (25 °C) and elevated temperatures (450 °C). Through detailed microstructural, mechanical, and fractographic evaluations, the dual effects of HIP were revealed: a slight reduction in fatigue strength at room temperature but a pronounced improvement in fatigue resistance under high-temperature cyclic loading. The observed trends were linked to fundamental microstructural transformations induced by HIP, including recrystallization, porosity elimination, and twin boundary formation, which collectively enhanced thermal stability and fatigue reliability. Some key findings of this study can be listed as below:

  * 1.

Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) at 1150 °C/100 MPa for 4 h produced fully recrystallized, equiaxed grains with Σ3 twin boundary fraction rising from ∼2.4 % to ∼33 %, and nearly eliminated porosity. HIP reduced yield stress and ultimate tensile strength due to the dissolution of cellular substructures and loss of work-hardening features, but it increased ductility significantly (up to ∼80 % elongation).

  * 2.

At an ambient temperature, as-built samples retained finer sub-grain features and higher dislocation densities, providing a higher endurance limit (240 MPa vs. 220 MPa for HIP).

  * 3.

At 450 °C, HIP samples exhibited a higher endurance limit (170 MPa vs. 130 MPa) and enhanced fatigue life retention due to enhanced thermal stability and twin boundary strengthening.

  * 4.

Failures in as-built samples were dominated by multiple defect-driven crack initiation sites, while HIP specimens showed more stable crack growth from a single initiation point, improving fatigue reliability.

  * 5.

HIP microstructures resisted grain coarsening and dislocation accumulation at the elevated temperature, reducing susceptibility to creep-assisted crack growth and grain boundary sliding.

## Abstract

The cumulative effect of many incidents that are brought about by an increase in temperature establishes an environment in which premature failure (including fatigue failure) becomes a challenging issue. Isothermal rotating bending fatigue (IT-RBF) testing may simulate industrial components' high temperatures and rotating environments. This state-of-the-art review paper covers the current research on IT-RBF failure in wrought and additive-manufactured alloys, focusing on microstructural and lifetime models. The article emphasizes the need of using microstructural information in fatigue life models to better represent complex material structure-failure behavior associations. Additive-manufactured alloys contain unique microstructural characteristics and processing-induced defects making fatigue modeling difficult. The paper concludes with implications for industrial fatigue-resistant alloy development. It emphasizes the necessity for a multidisciplinary approach that integrates materials science, mechanics, and data science to optimize these materials under cyclic loads. The review concludes by proposing future research and innovation in this subject.
